newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CENTRISTS REJECT PACT WITH LEFT OR RIGHT.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CENTRISTS REJECT PACT WITH LEFT OR RIGHT.

text.p: The chief of Poland's centrist Union for Freedom (UW) party on Thursday rejected a coalition with either the ruling ex-communists or the powerful right-leaning opposition led by the Solidarity union.

"These groupings are very similar conglomerates, which merely have different names. It is hard to say which of these two plagues would be worse for Poland," UW leader Leszek Balcerowicz said in comments quoted by PAP news agency.

Poland's next parliamentary elections, due around September, are likely to be dominated by the clash between the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of former communists and their bitter foes the rightist Solidarity Election Action (AWS).

The two giants are competing for a clear lead in opinion polls which show they may each gain about one third of parliamentary seats, meaning smaller parties like the UW may be crucial to forming a coalition that can govern.
Although its support is much smaller, the UW groups many of the intellectuals who helped steer the pre-1989 opposition to communist rule and formed the first democratic governments.

UW leader Balcerowicz, who made his comments to students in the southern city of Katowice, was the finance minister who steered Poland's radical shock-therapy reforms widely credited with laying the foundations for present economic growth.
The ex-communists would love to lure the Union for Freedom into a coalition, a "historic compromise" which would help them shed the stigma of their origins in the repressive old system.
But Balcerowicz spurned their approaches and rejected SLD suggestions that they had many policies in common.
"The SLD is trying to attach itself to us and offer its cheek for a kiss," PAP quoted him as saying.
"But in practice huge differences divide us, in policies and regarding our will to pursue reforms," Balcerowicz said.

He accused the ex-communists of being chiefly interested in looking after their own supporters. He said they had only tackled crucial reforms such as the pension system or privatisation of the telecommunications monopoly at the end of their four years of coalition governments with a Peasant party.

Some supporters of the AWS would also like a coalition with the UW, which has many experts and would reassure voters that the union-led alliance, which has some radical populist factions, would pursue market reforms.
But Balcerowicz is also contemptuous of the AWS, which includes estranged former allies. He savaged its election programme as incoherent when it was announced last month.
While the UW's tactics allow it to keep its principles pure, critics wonder if it has any future on its own.
Its famous names, heroes of the democracy movement such as Tadeusz Mazowiecki and Jacek Kuron, are fading from politics.
Mazowiecki, the first democratically-elected prime minister after 1989, may not stand in the elections although party spokesman Andrzej Potocki said it would ask him to reconsider.
Kuron, who is Poland's most popular politician, has kept a low profile in recent months and has had some health problems.
